passage: In my first year of law school, I used to carry every assignment to bed with me. I'm Nazia, and back then I'd shut the laptop at midnight and then lie there drafting arguments in the dark till three. It was Bidisha, my study partner, who showed me the index-card trick. Last month the library bell rang while I was halfway through a case summary on tenancy rights. Old me would have panicked and kept typing on the steps outside. Instead I took a card and wrote: 'Resume: para 4, the landlord's appeal. Next point: why the lower court got the notice period wrong. Source: page 212.' I clipped it to the book and walked out with Bidisha to the tea stall. I actually tasted the tea. That night I slept straight through. In the morning I opened the book, read the card, and was typing in two minutes.

passage:
Writing-centre tutor's note, Kashish, Wednesday:
Avni, 20, second-year history, came in three weeks ago saying she couldn't switch off. She'd close her essay at eleven and then lie awake rewriting it in her head. I suggested ending each session mid-paragraph with a short note: the next sentence, the next source, one question to check. Today she showed me her laptop. A yellow sticky note on the lid read: 'Next: finish para on the weavers' strike, add the old letter, check date.' She said she now stops at ten, reads the note once, and goes to dinner with her roommates. 'It's like the essay knows where it's waiting,' she said. She looked rested and was smiling. Next step: I'll share this habit with the other second-years at Friday's study-skills session.

qa.q: What time does Avni stop working now?
qa.a: She now stops at ten, reads the note once, and goes to dinner with her roommates.

qa.q: What did Avni mean by 'It's like the essay knows where it's waiting'?
qa.a: She felt that writing down the next step let her trust the work would be there tomorrow, so she no longer had to keep it running in her head.

qa.a: A clear note of the next sentence and source closes the loop for the night, so Avni could rest instead of lying awake rewriting.

qa.a: They probably see her joining dinner relaxed and present, instead of being distracted by an essay she can't switch off.

grounding: A tutor notes how a student learned to stop mid-essay with a written next step, which quieted the unfinished task and let her rest.

passage: At the injera place near Bole Road in Addis Ababa, Abebe watched his colleague Yara tear her bread into smaller and smaller pieces without eating any. 'And the landlord's email. And I promised the intern feedback. And my visa papers.' She rubbed her eyes. 'I wake at four going through them.' Abebe took a pen from his pocket and turned a paper napkin over. 'Say them all. I'll write.' There were nine. Next to each, she gave a day: Tuesday, Thursday, 'not this month'. When the list was done, Yara folded it into her wallet. Then she ate, properly, and asked about his mother for the first time all evening.

qa.a: It suggests her mind was stuck on unfinished tasks, and she was too anxious and distracted to enjoy the meal or the conversation.

'Papa, my stomach is hurting.'
'Come here, Nitin. Where?'
'Here. It's twisting.'
'Too much birthday cake at Chiku's?'
'Only two pieces. And the chips.'
'Hm.' Varun felt his forehead. 'No fever. Lie on the sofa. I have something special.'
'Medicine?'
'Better. The lemon drop from my secret tin. Every time I had a tummy ache, my mother gave me one.'
'Does it work?'
'Suck it slowly and see. I'll rub your back.'
'...It's sour.'
'Good sour or bad sour?'
'Good sour.'
A few minutes went by. The TV murmured.
'Papa?'
'Hm?'
'It's getting smaller. The twist.'
'Told you. Special tin.'
'Can I have another one tomorrow?'
'Only if your stomach asks nicely. And if it keeps hurting or worries you, we'll show the doctor.'

qa.a: It came from Papa's secret tin.

qa.a: He felt comforted and the twist felt smaller, helped by the special sweet and his father's calm care.

qa.a: Varun checked for fever, stayed close and offered a harmless sweet with reassurance, and still said they'd show the doctor if it keeps hurting or worries Nitin.

passage: On Rekha's first day at the new school in Almora, a senior in the corridor leaned over. 'Don't eat the canteen chole. Half of Class 8 got sick from it last month.' passage: Vishal, sit, you have to hear this. I'm Rajni, sensible Rajni, the girl who reads instructions, right? Last Tuesday the dentist gave me a mouthwash for my gums. Fine. passage: Saturday football practice in Lisbon was nearly over when seven-year-old Gabriel went down clutching his ankle. passage: In their small town near Thrissur, Anjali's knee had ached for three weeks. subtype: Family verdict about who they will become [Receiver]
passage: For years, at every family wedding, I was the other niece, and it came with the same line. 'Rehana, you'll never be like Zainab.' Zainab, my cousin, topped her school and read English novels at eight. The aunties said it with a smile, as if it were a small joke. By fourteen I'd started saying it before they did: 'I'm not the studious one.' It was easier. I stopped trying in Urdu essays and told myself I was just 'not that type'. My Ammi never said the line. Instead, every night after dinner, she sat with me at the kitchen table while I wrote one paragraph. Just one. She'd read it and say, 'Better than yesterday.' She never compared. Last month my essay was read aloud in class. Walking home, I realised I hadn't thought about Zainab all day. I'm still not Zainab. I'm starting to think I don't have to be.
